cards.front: In the vertebrate retina, the {{c1::ganglion cells}} are the only output to the brain, and they fire action potentials.
cards.back: Their axons gather at the optic disk to form the optic nerve.
cards.quote: Ganglion cells fire action potentials. The ganglion cells are the retina's only output.

cards.front: Which retinal cells signal mainly with graded potentials rather than spikes?
cards.back: Photoreceptors, horizontal cells and most bipolar cells. Their voltage varies smoothly with input, and no spike is needed over such short distances.
cards.quote: Photoreceptors, horizontal cells and most bipolar cells signal with graded potentials, voltage changes that vary smoothly with input and need no spike over these short distances

cards.front: The retina's organizing rule: one receptor cannot separate wavelength from {{c1::intensity}}; the circuit compares.
cards.quote: One receptor cannot separate wavelength from intensity; the circuit compares.

cards.front: What holds the outer-segment channels of a photoreceptor open in darkness, and what ions carry the dark current?
cards.back: cGMP, made by guanylyl cyclase, holds the CNG channels open. Sodium and calcium flow in; the current leaves again at the inner segment.
cards.quote: In darkness, cGMP made by guanylyl cyclase holds open cyclic-nucleotide-gated (CNG) channels in the outer segment.

cards.front: Why does closing a cation channel make a photoreceptor more negative?
cards.back: In the lesson's fixed-conductance sketch with no injected current, the voltage moves toward a conductance-weighted balance point of the reversal potentials. CNG channels pull toward about 0 mV, potassium toward E_K. Removing the CNG pull moves the balance point toward E_K, so potassium is in charge and the cell hyperpolarizes.
cards.quote: So closing a channel can make a cell more negative: removing the inward cation pull leaves potassium in charge.
cards.section: Why closing channels makes the cell more negative

cards.front: In the photoreceptor sketch with equal CNG and potassium conductances in the dark, the balance point sits at about {{c1::−40 mV}}.
cards.back: Halfway between the CNG reversal near 0 mV and E_K, about −80 mV in the sketch.
cards.quote: The balance point then sits halfway, at about −40 mV, the textbook dark potential of a photoreceptor.
cards.section: Why closing channels makes the cell more negative

cards.front: Photoreceptor sketch: CNG channels reverse at 0 mV, E_K = −80 mV, and the two conductances are equal in the dark. Light closes 75% of the CNG channels; potassium conductance is unchanged. What is the new balance point?
cards.back: Vm = (0.25 × 0 + 1 × −80) / (0.25 + 1) = −80 / 1.25 = −64 mV. The cell hyperpolarizes toward E_K but stops short of −80 mV, which needs all CNG channels shut.
cards.quote: Vm = (g_CNG × 0 mV + g_K × E_K) / (g_CNG + g_K)
cards.section: Why closing channels makes the cell more negative

cards.front: A photon absorbed by rhodopsin isomerizes its chromophore, retinal, from {{c1::11-cis}} to all-trans, activating the pigment.
cards.quote: isomerizes its chromophore, the light-absorbing retinal, changing its shape from 11-cis to all-trans.

cards.front: In phototransduction, which enzyme lowers cGMP, and which G protein activates it?
cards.back: PDE6, a phosphodiesterase that hydrolyzes cGMP. It is activated by transducin.
cards.quote: Transducin activates PDE6, a phosphodiesterase. PDE6 hydrolyzes cGMP, so cGMP falls.

cards.front: Where does much of the amplification (gain) in rod phototransduction come from?
cards.back: One activated pigment molecule activates many transducins.
cards.quote: One activated pigment activates many transducins, which is where much of the amplification, or gain, comes from.

cards.front: How does the fall in outer-segment calcium after a flash speed a photoreceptor's recovery?
cards.back: With CNG channels closed, less calcium enters while extrusion continues. Low calcium lets GCAPs stimulate guanylyl cyclase, which remakes cGMP and reopens the channels.
cards.quote: Low calcium lets GCAPs (guanylyl cyclase-activating proteins) stimulate the cyclase, which remakes cGMP and speeds recovery.

cards.front: A rod's PDE6 is inactive. A bright flash is absorbed by its rhodopsin. Predict cGMP, the CNG channels, the membrane potential and glutamate release.
cards.back: cGMP stays high, the CNG channels stay open, the rod stays depolarized and glutamate release stays at its dark level.
cards.why: PDE6 is the step that hydrolyzes cGMP; without it, transducin activation cannot reach the channels.
cards.quote: PDE6 hydrolyzes cGMP, so cGMP falls. CNG channels close. The dark current shrinks, the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes, and glutamate release falls.

cards.front: Rods are engineered to lack GCAPs. Predict their recovery after a flash, and their gain in steady bright light.
cards.back: Recovery is slower, because falling calcium can no longer stimulate the cyclase to remake cGMP. In steady light the gain is turned down less, so this part of light adaptation is weakened.
cards.quote: In steadier, brighter light the same feedback turns the gain down, part of light adaptation

cards.front: A mutation locks a rod's CNG channels open whatever the cGMP level. In dim light, predict the rod's voltage, its glutamate release, and the responses of the ON and OFF bipolar cells it drives.
cards.back: The rod stays depolarized and keeps releasing glutamate at the dark level. Its glutamate signal never changes, so the light-driven responses it would drive stay absent: ON bipolar cells (mGluR6) stay hyperpolarized and OFF bipolar cells stay depolarized, and in the rod pathway (ON rod bipolar to AII cell) there is no rod-driven depolarization of ON cone bipolars or hyperpolarization of OFF cone bipolars.
cards.why: The dark current sets glutamate release, and each bipolar cell's receptor only reads changes in that release.
cards.quote: It keeps the cell depolarized and releasing glutamate at its terminal.

cards.front: A toad rod outer segment is drawn into a suction electrode and a very dim flash is repeated many times. The histogram of response sizes has a peak at zero and a peak near 1 pA. What does this show?
cards.back: Responses come in discrete units. Each unit, about 1 pA, is the current suppressed by one photoisomerization, one pigment molecule activated by one photon.
cards.quote: a histogram of their sizes has a peak at zero and a peak near 1 pA.

cards.front: Doubling a dim flash on a toad rod doubles the mean response. Why does the size of the unit response stay about the same?
cards.back: Each unit is still one photoisomerization, about 1 pA. A stronger flash makes more trials respond and more of them carry two events.
cards.quote: The unit stays about 1 pA, because each event is still one photoisomerization.

cards.front: Dim flashes on a toad rod give on average m = 2 photoisomerizations. Capture is Poisson and each event gives 1 pA, adding linearly. What fraction of flashes fail, what fraction give exactly one event, and what is the mean response?
cards.back: P(0) = e^−2 = 0.135, so about 14% fail. P(1) = 2 × e^−2 = 0.271, about 27%. Mean response = 2 × 1 pA = 2 pA.
cards.quote: the chance that a flash gives exactly k events follows a Poisson distribution, P(k) = m^k × e^−m / k!

cards.front: A dim flash is given 400 times to a toad rod in a suction electrode, and 50 trials show no response. Assuming Poisson capture and 1 pA per event, estimate the mean number of photoisomerizations per flash and the mean response.
cards.back: P(0) = 50/400 = 0.125. m = −ln(0.125) ≈ 2.1 photoisomerizations, so the mean response is about 2.1 pA.
cards.quote: Run it backwards and the failure rate gives the mean: m = −ln P(0).

cards.front: Use the Poisson rule to explain why the rod pathway pools many rods onto each rod bipolar cell and AII amacrine cell. Take a dim flash giving on average 0.5 photoisomerizations per rod.
cards.back: P(0) = e^−0.5 ≈ 0.61, so most rods catch nothing on a given flash and any one rod's report is mostly zero. Summing many rods collects the scarce events, at the cost of spatial detail.
cards.why: Rests on Poisson photon capture and on convergence pooling scarce photons.
cards.quote: Many rods feed each rod bipolar cell, and many rod bipolar cells feed each AII: this is where the pooling happens.

cards.front: Photoreceptors release only glutamate. How can it depolarize some bipolar cells and hyperpolarize others?
cards.back: The receptor sets the sign. OFF bipolar cells use ionotropic AMPA or kainate receptors (sign preserved); ON bipolar cells use the metabotropic mGluR6 (sign inverted).
cards.quote: Glutamate's sign is set by the receptor, not the molecule

cards.front: In mammalian ON bipolar cells in the dark, glutamate-bound mGluR6 activates Go, which keeps the cation channel {{c1::TRPM1}} closed.
cards.quote: In the dark, glutamate-bound mGluR6 activates the G protein Go, which keeps the cation channel TRPM1 closed.

cards.front: Light falls on the cones that drive a mammalian ON bipolar cell. Trace why the bipolar cell depolarizes.
cards.back: Cones hyperpolarize and release less glutamate. Less mGluR6 activation lowers Go activity, so TRPM1 cation channels open and the cell depolarizes.
cards.quote: Light lowers glutamate, Go activity declines, TRPM1 opens and the cell depolarizes.

cards.front: Using the count-the-inversions rule, why does an OFF bipolar cell respond like darkness and an ON bipolar cell like light?
cards.back: The photoreceptor gives one inversion. The OFF bipolar adds none (odd total, like darkness); the ON bipolar adds a second (even total, like light).
cards.quote: The OFF bipolar cell adds none, so it responds like darkness.

cards.front: Suppose a bipolar cell's glutamate receptor were an inhibitory channel, one that hyperpolarizes the cell when glutamate binds. Would the cell respond to light on its cones as an ON or an OFF cell?
cards.back: ON. Glutamate inhibits it in the dark; light lowers glutamate, removes the inhibition, and the cell depolarizes.
cards.why: The receptor sets the sign. This receptor adds a second inversion, and an even count means the cell responds like light.
cards.quote: The ON bipolar cell adds a second, and an even number means the cell responds like light.

cards.front: In a mudpuppy eyecup, APB, a glutamate analogue acting at the ON receptor, abolished ON bipolar light responses and spared OFF responses. What does this show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: The ON pathway reads glutamate through a distinct receptor; APB holds ON cells in their dark state. It does not identify the receptor or the channel.
cards.quote: APB shows only that the ON pathway uses a distinct receptor; it does not name the receptor or the channel
cards.section: The evidence: one drug, one pathway

cards.front: APB abolishes ON bipolar light responses in a perfused eyecup. Which controls show this is a receptor effect rather than a damaged retina?
cards.back: OFF responses persist in the same retina, and ON responses recover after washout.
cards.quote: The OFF responses in the same retina, and recovery after washout, are the controls that show a receptor effect rather than a damaged retina.
cards.section: The evidence: one drug, one pathway

cards.front: APB is applied while recording an ON-centre and an OFF-centre ganglion cell in daylight conditions. A spot is flashed on each cell's centre. Predict both responses.
cards.back: The ON-centre cell loses its light response; the OFF-centre cell still responds.
cards.why: APB holds ON bipolar cells in their dark state. ON bipolar cells drive ON ganglion cells, and OFF bipolar cells drive OFF ganglion cells.
cards.quote: ON bipolar cells drive ON ganglion cells, and OFF bipolar cells drive OFF ganglion cells.
cards.section: The evidence: one drug, one pathway

cards.front: A ganglion cell's {{c1::receptive field}} is the patch of retina where light changes its firing.
cards.quote: A ganglion cell's receptive field is the patch of retina where light changes its firing.

cards.front: How does an ON-centre ganglion cell respond to a light spot in its centre, and to a ring of light on its surround?
cards.back: Centre spot: it fires faster. Surround ring: its firing is suppressed (in Kuffler's recording it fell silent, then fired when the light went off).
cards.quote: A spot a little farther out, on a ring around the middle: the same cell falls silent, then fires when the light goes off.

cards.front: Which retinal cells build a ganglion cell's receptive-field centre, and which build its surround?
cards.back: The centre comes from bipolar cells contacting its dendrites. The surround comes from lateral cells: horizontal cells feeding back onto cone terminals, plus amacrine inhibition in the inner retina.
cards.quote: The centre comes from the bipolar cells that contact the ganglion cell's dendrites. The surround comes from lateral cells.
cards.section: Where centre and surround come from

cards.front: Why does an ON-centre ganglion cell fire less to light covering its whole receptive field than to a spot filling only its centre?
cards.back: Light on the surround subtracts from the centre's excitation. The cell therefore reports contrast more than overall light level.
cards.quote: The cell reports contrast, a spot brighter than its surroundings, more than overall light level.
cards.section: Where centre and surround come from

cards.front: A made-up ON-centre ganglion cell fires 12 spikes/s on a grey background, 42 spikes/s to a spot filling its centre, and 4 spikes/s to an annulus on its surround. Assuming linear addition, predict the rate for light covering both, and the net change from background.
cards.back: Centre effect = 42 − 12 = +30; surround effect = 4 − 12 = −8. Both: 12 + 30 − 8 = 34 spikes/s, a net change of +22 spikes/s.
cards.quote: Step 3. Light covering both: 20 + 40 − 15 = 45 spikes/s, less than the spot's 60.
cards.section: Where centre and surround come from

cards.front: A light spot centred on an ON-centre ganglion cell grows from tiny to the full field. In a standard model with a surround weaker than the centre, how does the firing rate change?
cards.back: It rises, peaks for a spot about the size of the centre, then falls as the spot spreads into the surround, settling above the background rate.
cards.quote: the response rises, peaks for a spot about the size of the centre, then falls as the spot spreads into the surround.
cards.section: Where centre and surround come from

cards.front: A row of ON-centre ganglion cells lies across a light-dark edge. Which cells fire most, and which fire least?
cards.back: Most: cells centred just on the bright side, because their surrounds reach into the dark and subtract less. Least: cells centred just on the dark side.
cards.why: OFF-centre cells show the mirror image.
cards.quote: Cells whose centres sit just on the bright side of an edge fire more than cells in the middle of a bright area
cards.section: Edges stand out across the population

cards.front: In a linear model with a symmetric field, an ON-centre cell fires 20 spikes/s in uniform dark and 45 spikes/s in uniform bright light. What does it fire when centred exactly on a light-dark edge?
cards.back: Half its centre and half its surround are lit, so its change is half the bright-field change: 20 + (45 − 20)/2 = 32.5 spikes/s.
cards.quote: its change from the uniform-dark rate is half the full bright-field change.
cards.section: Edges stand out across the population

cards.front: In a linear model, suppose an ON-centre cell's surround cancelled its centre exactly. What would uniform light do to its rate, and would edges still stand out across the population?
cards.back: Uniform light would leave the cell at its background rate. Edges would still stand out: near an edge, centre and surround are lit unequally, so those cells move away from background while cells in uniform areas do not.
cards.why: Rests on linear centre-surround addition and the edge rule that a surround reaching into the dark subtracts less.
cards.quote: In this linear model, uniform light would leave the cell at its 20 spikes/s background only if the surround cancelled the centre exactly.
cards.section: Where centre and surround come from

cards.front: Compare rods with cones in sensitivity, speed and convergence.
cards.back: Rods are more sensitive and slower, and many rods converge onto each downstream cell, pooling photons at the cost of spatial detail.
cards.quote: Rods are more sensitive than cones and respond more slowly, trading temporal resolution for sensitivity.

cards.front: A human retina has about {{c1::20}} rods for every cone, so rods make up about 95% of photoreceptors.
cards.back: Cones dominate the fovea; rods are absent from its very centre.
cards.quote: In a human retina there are about 20 rods for every cone, and rods make up about 95% of photoreceptors

cards.front: In the primary mammalian rod pathway, how does the AII amacrine cell pass rod signals to ON and to OFF cone bipolar cells, and with what sign?
cards.back: To ON cone bipolars through gap junctions: sign kept, they depolarize. To OFF cone bipolars through glycine synapses: inhibitory, sign inverted, they hyperpolarize.
cards.quote: To OFF cone bipolar cells through glycine synapses. Glycine is inhibitory, so the OFF cone bipolar cell hyperpolarizes.

cards.front: A drug blocks the gap junctions between AII amacrine cells and ON cone bipolar cells. In very dim light, which ganglion cells lose most of their rod-driven response?
cards.back: ON ganglion cells. The AII's route to OFF cone bipolars, a glycine synapse, is intact, so OFF cells keep their rod-driven response.
cards.why: Rests on the primary rod circuit as drawn; secondary rod routes may carry some signal.
cards.quote: To ON cone bipolar cells through gap junctions. Current passes straight through, so the ON cone bipolar cell depolarizes too.

cards.front: APB, which mimics glutamate at mGluR6, is applied in very dim, rod-only light. Which ganglion cells lose most of their rod-driven response: ON, OFF, or both?
cards.back: Both. Rod bipolar cells are ON cells that read glutamate through mGluR6, so APB holds them in their dark state, and both ON and OFF rod signals pass through rod bipolar cells to the AII.
cards.why: Combines APB's action on the ON receptor with the primary rod pathway. Secondary rod routes may still carry some signal.
cards.quote: Rod bipolar cells read glutamate through mGluR6, so they are ON cells.

cards.front: Count sign inversions along the primary rod pathway from rod to OFF cone bipolar cell. Show the result matches the cone-to-OFF-bipolar pathway.
cards.back: Rod hyperpolarizes (−); rod bipolar via mGluR6 depolarizes (+); AII, excited by glutamate, depolarizes (+); glycine onto the OFF cone bipolar hyperpolarizes it (−). Net −, the same as cone (−) to OFF bipolar (no flip).
cards.why: So one ganglion cell gives the same ON or OFF report whether rods or cones drive it.
cards.quote: So one ganglion cell can carry rod signals at night and cone signals by day, and the brain receives ON and OFF reports either way.

cards.front: State the principle of univariance and why it means a single cone cannot report colour.
cards.back: Wavelength changes only the probability that a photon is caught, and a change in intensity can mimic that; an absorbed photon carries no wavelength label. With intensities chosen to give the same effective catch, timing and adaptation, a dim light near the cone's peak and a brighter one far from it give indistinguishable responses on average (single trials stay noisy).
cards.quote: Wavelength changes only the probability that a photon is caught, and a change in intensity can mimic that.

cards.front: Why does the ratio of M-cone to L-cone catch carry wavelength information that a single cone cannot?
cards.back: The M and L curves differ, so the ratio varies with wavelength. Turning the light up or down changes both catches together, so the ratio holds.
cards.quote: Turn a light up or down and both catches change together, so the ratio holds

cards.front: In standard pigment templates, lights near 427 nm and 529 nm give the same M/L catch ratio. Their intensities are set so their L catches match. Can a person with only M and L cones tell them apart? What lets a trichromat do so?
cards.back: No: with L catches matched, the M catches match too. The S cone catches far more at 427 nm than at 529 nm and breaks the tie.
cards.quote: Adjust their intensities so their L catches match, and their M catches match too, so M and L cones alone would confuse them.

cards.front: In very dim light only rods respond, and all rods use the same pigment, rhodopsin. Using the lesson's rules, explain why such vision cannot report colour.
cards.back: Each rod's response keeps no record of wavelength, and with a single receptor class there is no second sensitivity curve to compare. Rod signals feed ON and OFF lines, which report contrast, not colour.
cards.why: Rests on univariance and on colour as a comparison across receptor classes.
cards.quote: Once absorbed, every photon has the same effect, whatever its wavelength.

cards.front: TRPM1-deficient mice are compared with controls by electroretinogram. What result places the defect after photoreceptor activation, in ON bipolar cells?
cards.back: A normal a-wave (mainly photoreceptor current) with an absent b-wave (mainly ON bipolar activity).
cards.why: If photoreceptors failed to transduce light, the a-wave would be lost too.
cards.quote: The a-wave, mainly photoreceptor current, was normal; the b-wave, mainly ON bipolar activity, was absent.

cards.front: Rod bipolar cells from germline TRPM1 knockout mice lack light-evoked current. Why is this not enough to show TRPM1 is the channel light opens, and what experiments would strengthen the case?
cards.back: The knockout could act in development, for example on synapse formation: check the synapse is built, or delete the gene only in adults. Rescue TRPM1 in ON bipolar cells. Loss shows necessity; test sufficiency by expressing TRPM1 with mGluR6 and Go in another cell.
cards.quote: A germline knockout can act during development, for example by changing synapse formation, so a missing current might not mean the channel itself is gone
